title: Every sound is a sum of circles

scenes.narration: Pluck a guitar string and the air beside your ear starts to wiggle. Plot that air pressure over time and you get a messy scribble. Yet hidden inside it is something astonishingly simple.

props.text: Every sound is a wiggle in the air

scenes.narration: Meet the simplest motion there is: an arrow spinning at a steady pace. Ignore everything except the height of its tip, and that height rises and falls as a perfectly smooth wave. That is a pure tone.

props.text: One spinning arrow, one pure tone

scenes.narration: Every spinning arrow has exactly two dials. Its length sets how far the tip swings, which we hear as loudness. Its speed sets how often the wave repeats, which we hear as pitch. Spin three times faster and the tone jumps up in pitch.

Now the trick. Stack the arrows tip to tail and let each one spin at its own speed. The tip of the last arrow is the sum of all of them. Its height no longer traces a plain wave; it traces something with shoulders and corners.

With the right lengths and speeds, circles can even build a square wave. One circle gives a gentle hump. Three circles start to square the shoulders. Twelve circles hug the target closely, apart from a small overshoot that lingers right at each jump. This is Fourier's bold claim: a repeating signal is a sum of circles.

props.text: Even sharp corners are made of circles

scenes.narration: Now free the tip to move in two dimensions instead of just up and down. Treat each point on a drawing as a complex number, and the very same chain of spinning circles can trace a heart, a signature, almost any closed outline.

The Fourier transform runs this recipe in reverse. Hand it the messy wiggle and it reports how long the arrow must be at every possible speed: a spectrum. Here it finds three spikes, three pure tones hiding inside one sound.

props.text: The Fourier transform runs the recipe backward

props.tex: \hat f(\xi) = \int f(t)\, e^{-2\pi i \xi t}\, dt

scenes.narration: Your inner ear does a version of this, sorting incoming sound by pitch along a coiled membrane. Audio and image compression lean on Fourier-style transforms, and MRI scanners rebuild pictures from frequency data. Every sound is a sum of circles; the Fourier transform tells you which ones.

props.text: Every sound is a sum of circles.
